name: Pranic therapy

lead: Pranic therapy, usually called pranic healing, is a complementary practice in which a practitioner works on the energy body that its followers say surrounds and controls the physical body, using the hands without touching.

Its link to appearance is indirect and claimed: supporters connect better wellbeing, stress relief and sleep with a healthier, more rested look. A handful of small randomized trials have tested it as an add-on therapy for conditions such as depression, urinary symptoms and foot ulcers.

paras: Sessions are delivered by trained practitioners who pass their hands over the body, and the same system includes meditations such as Meditation on Twin Hearts. It is generally used alongside conventional care.

The practice itself involves no substances or physical manipulation. Reviews note that reliance on it in place of medical care is the main concern, and meditation-based practices have been associated in case reports with psychotic episodes in a small number of people.

chain: Claimed relaxation, better sleep and mood
angle.text: Practitioners describe pranic healing as balancing the body's energy, which followers associate with calm and wellbeing. Any appearance benefit is an indirect claim tied to rest and stress levels.

lead: Pranic healing is described by its proponents as a science and art of healing that treats the energy body, said to interpenetrate and control the physical body, mind and emotions.[1] Prana is a Sanskrit term for life force.[2]

Followers use it for general wellbeing, stress and recovery. In looksmaxxing-adjacent circles it appears as a fringe, hands-off 'healing' practice; any effect on appearance would run through claimed improvements in calm, sleep and health rather than a direct change to the face or body.

Reviews written within holistic nursing argue for its introduction into clinical nursing practice,[3] while research reviews describe the field of biofield practices, including pranic healing, as having methodological challenges.[4] Several small randomized trials have tested pranic healing as an add-on to standard care.[5][6][7]
infobox: Prana (life force) and the energy body[1]

paras: Pranic healing treats a claimed energy body. Its literature says that applying the technique can alter the molecular structure of liquid and dense matter, an assertion proponents point to research for.[1] Nursing papers present it as an energy-based complementary technique that could promote client wellbeing.[3]

The system includes a guided meditation, Meditation on Twin Hearts, with components of lovingkindness, open awareness and self-healing imagery, which has been studied for effects on brain event-related potentials.[8]

Reviews of biofield modalities, which include qigong, Reiki, therapeutic touch and pranic healing, report preclinical studies in which proponents say biofields affect biological systems, and discuss methodological issues in such work.[4] A 2023 qualitative meta-synthesis collected nineteen studies of how people experience 'prana' and biofield therapies.[9]
Mainstream encyclopedic sources state there is no scientific evidence for a vital energy of this kind, and that energy-therapy claims rest mostly on anecdote.[2]

A narrative review of case reports describes psychotic states triggered or worsened in association with meditative practice in some people, though meditation is also associated with health benefits.[10]

A randomized trial of 76 men with lower urinary tract symptoms compared medication with medication plus pranic healing, examining urinary symptoms and sleep.[5] A double-blind trial of 52 people with mild to moderate depression compared medication plus pranic healing with medication plus mock pranic healing over five weeks.[6] A randomized double-blind trial examined it as a complementary therapy in diabetic foot ulcer management, and a later corrigendum was published.[7] A trial in children tested a pranic-healing approach based on therapeutic touch for pain and cardiorespiratory indices during venipuncture.[11] A preliminary placebo-controlled trial examined the time taken to sense a biofield between the hands.[12]
